display.text:
name: Promote main to production

# Promotes the latest main commit to production via immutable SHA tags.
#
# Auth, Core, and MCP share a monorepo and must advance atomically in
# production. All three images are built and scanned first; none is published
# until all three have passed. The publish job pushes the 'main' tag and a
# sha-<commit> tag back-to-back, then verifies all registry manifests, so
# the promotion commit never references an image that does not exist.
#
# Only push events to main trigger this workflow. Pull-request runs cannot
# publish or promote images. The bot-commit guard prevents promotion loops
# when the promotion commit itself triggers a new run.

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: write
  packages: write

env:
  MAIN_TAG: main
  SHA_TAG: sha-${{ github.sha }}

jobs:
  build-auth:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Build auth image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile.auth
          pull: true
          # Refresh Debian security packages without discarding the dependency build cache.
          no-cache-filters: runtime
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          platforms: linux/amd64
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'
          ignore-unfixed: true

      - name: Save image
        run: docker save -o auth-image.tar "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}"

      - name: Upload auth image
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: auth-image
          path: auth-image.tar

  build-core:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Build core image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          pull: true
          # Refresh Debian security packages without discarding the dependency build cache.
          no-cache-filters: runtime
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          platforms: linux/amd64
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'
          ignore-unfixed: true

      - name: Save image
        run: docker save -o core-image.tar "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}"

      - name: Upload core image
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: core-image
          path: core-image.tar

  build-mcp:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Build MCP image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile.mcp
          pull: true
          # Refresh Debian security packages without discarding the dependency build cache.
          no-cache-filters: runtime
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          platforms: linux/amd64
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'
          ignore-unfixed: true

      - name: Save image
        run: docker save -o mcp-image.tar "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${{ env.MAIN_TAG }}"

      - name: Upload MCP image
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: mcp-image
          path: mcp-image.tar

  promote:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [build-auth, build-core, build-mcp]
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'push' &&
      github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' &&
      startsWith(github.actor, 'github-actions[bot]') == false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Download images
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v7
        with:
          pattern: "*-image"
          path: images

      - name: Load images
        run: |
          docker load -i images/auth-image/auth-image.tar
          docker load -i images/core-image/core-image.tar
          docker load -i images/mcp-image/mcp-image.tar

      - name: Login to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push all images
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          docker tag "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${MAIN_TAG}" "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${SHA_TAG}"
          docker tag "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${MAIN_TAG}" "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${SHA_TAG}"
          docker tag "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${MAIN_TAG}" "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${SHA_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${MAIN_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth:${SHA_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${MAIN_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core:${SHA_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${MAIN_TAG}"
          docker push "ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp:${SHA_TAG}"

      - name: Verify all registry manifests
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          for repo in calendar-auth calendar-core calendar-mcp; do
            token=$(curl -s "https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:david-hajnal/${repo}:pull" | jq -r .token)
            curl -sf -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" \
              "https://ghcr.io/v2/david-hajnal/${repo}/manifests/${MAIN_TAG}" >/dev/null
            echo "OK: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/${repo}:${MAIN_TAG} manifest present"
          done

      - name: Verify all sha-<commit> manifests
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          for repo in calendar-auth calendar-core calendar-mcp; do
            token=$(curl -s "https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:david-hajnal/${repo}:pull" | jq -r .token)
            curl -sf -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" \
              "https://ghcr.io/v2/david-hajnal/${repo}/manifests/${SHA_TAG}" >/dev/null
            echo "OK: ghcr.io/david-hajnal/${repo}:${SHA_TAG} manifest present"
          done

      - name: Promote immutable image tags
        env:
          SOURCE_SHA: ${{ github.sha }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git fetch origin main
          if [[ "$(git rev-parse origin/main)" != "${SOURCE_SHA}" ]]; then
            echo "A newer main commit exists; its workflow will promote that revision."
            exit 0
          fi

          promoted_tag="sha-${SOURCE_SHA}"
          for manifest in \
            deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml \
            deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/core-helmrelease.yaml \
            deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/mcp-helmrelease.yaml; do
            sed -i -E "s/^([[:space:]]*tag:).*/\\1 \"${promoted_tag}\"/" "${manifest}"
          done

          test "$(grep -hE "^[[:space:]]*tag: \"${promoted_tag}\"$" \
            deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/*-helmrelease.yaml | wc -l | tr -d ' ')" -eq 3

          git config user.name github-actions[bot]
          git config user.email 41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com
          git add deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/*-helmrelease.yaml
          git commit -m "chore(deploy): promote ${SOURCE_SHA}"
          git push origin HEAD:main

#   BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX   - hex-encoded backup encryption key (even hex, at least 32 chars; 64-hex backward-compatible)
#   MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY        - MCP internal API key
#   MCP_SESSION_SECRET          - MCP session secret
#   MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER            - HTTPS OAuth issuer exposing the JWKS endpoint
#   AUTH_DATABASE_URL           - PostgreSQL DSN for the authorization server (slice 5)
#   AUTH_BRIDGE_KEY             - shared secret for the private bridge (slice 5)
#   AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS            - comma-separated distinct cookie signing keys (slice 5)
#   AUTH_SIGNING_KID            - JWKS key ID for the authorization server (slice 5)
#   GITHUB_TOKEN                - GitHub PAT with repo write access
#   DOMAIN                      - core domain (default: cal.hajnal.space)
#   MCP_DOMAIN                  - MCP domain (default: mcal.hajnal.space)
#   NAMESPACE                   - k8s namespace (default: commoncal)
#   FLUX_OWNER                  - GitHub owner (default: david-hajnal)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Bootstrap production cluster with secrets and Flux.
#
# Required env vars:
#   SESSION_SECRET              - session encryption key
#   BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX   - hex-encoded backup encryption key (even hex, at least 32 chars; 64-hex backward-compatible)
#   MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY        - MCP internal API key
#   MCP_SESSION_SECRET          - MCP session secret
#   MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER            - HTTPS OAuth issuer exposing the JWKS endpoint
#   AUTH_DATABASE_URL           - PostgreSQL DSN for the authorization server (slice 5)
#   AUTH_BRIDGE_KEY             - shared secret for the private bridge (slice 5)
#   AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS            - comma-separated distinct cookie signing keys (slice 5)
#   AUTH_SIGNING_KID            - JWKS key ID for the authorization server (slice 5)
#   GITHUB_TOKEN                - GitHub PAT with repo write access
#   DOMAIN                      - core domain (default: cal.hajnal.space)
#   MCP_DOMAIN                  - MCP domain (default: mcal.hajnal.space)
#   NAMESPACE                   - k8s namespace (default: commoncal)
#   FLUX_OWNER                  - GitHub owner (default: david-hajnal)
#   FLUX_REPO                   - GitHub repo name (default: calendar)
#   FLUX_VERSION                - Flux toolkit version (default: v2.9.4)
#
# Optional env vars:
#   MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER_HOLD       - new issuer to HOLD (accept for validation)
#                                 without cutover (slice 5). If set, the MCP
#                                 server accepts tokens from both the primary
#                                 and held issuers.
#
# Values may be provided as environment variables or in deploy/.env (gitignored).
# Variables already set in the environment take precedence over the file.
#
# Usage:
#   ./deploy/bootstrap-production.sh
#   (or export the vars above / put them in deploy/.env)

# Load deploy/.env if present. Values already set in the environment win.
ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/.env"
if [[ -f "$ENV_FILE" ]]; then
  echo "==> Loading environment from $ENV_FILE"
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
    [[ -z "${line// }" ]] && continue
    [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]*# ]] && continue
    [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]*(export[[:space:]]+)?([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)=(.*)$ ]] || continue
    key="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
    value="${BASH_REMATCH[3]}"
    if [[ "$value" =~ ^\"(.*)\"$ ]]; then value="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"; fi
    if [[ "$value" =~ ^\'(.*)\'$ ]]; then value="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"; fi
    if [[ -z "${!key:-}" ]]; then
      export "$key=$value"
    fi
  done < "$ENV_FILE"
fi

NAMESPACE="${NAMESPACE:-commoncal}"
DOMAIN="${DOMAIN:-cal.hajnal.space}"
MCP_DOMAIN="${MCP_DOMAIN:-mcal.hajnal.space}"
FLUX_OWNER="${FLUX_OWNER:-david-hajnal}"
FLUX_REPO="${FLUX_REPO:-calendar}"
FLUX_VERSION="${FLUX_VERSION:-v2.9.4}"
TLS_SECRET_NAME="${TLS_SECRET_NAME:-commoncal-tls}"

echo "==> Validating required environment variables..."
for var in SESSION_SECRET BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY MCP_SESSION_SECRET MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER AUTH_DATABASE_URL AUTH_BRIDGE_KEY AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS AUTH_SIGNING_KID GITHUB_TOKEN; do
  if [[ -z "${!var:-}" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: $var is required" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done

if [[ ! "$BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX" =~ ^([[:xdigit:]]{2}){16,}$ ]]; then
  echo "ERROR: BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX must be an even number of hexadecimal characters (at least 32)" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Match the production runtime's comma-separated cookie-key rotation set.
if ! AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS="$AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS" python3 - <<'KEYS'
import os, sys
keys = [key.strip() for key in os.environ['AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS'].split(',')]
sys.exit(0 if len(keys) >= 2 and len(set(keys)) == len(keys) and all(len(key) >= 32 for key in keys) else 1)
KEYS
then
  echo "ERROR: AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS requires at least two distinct keys of 32+ characters" >&2
  exit 1
fi
: "${AUTH_JWKS_FILE:?AUTH_JWKS_FILE must point to the private production JWKS}"
[[ -r "$AUTH_JWKS_FILE" ]] || { echo 'ERROR: AUTH_JWKS_FILE is not readable' >&2; exit 1; }

# AUTH_DATABASE_URL must be a PostgreSQL DSN.
if [[ ! "$AUTH_DATABASE_URL" =~ ^postgres(ql)?:// ]]; then
  echo "ERROR: AUTH_DATABASE_URL must be a PostgreSQL DSN (postgres:// or postgresql://)" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "==> Ensuring namespace '$NAMESPACE' exists..."
kubectl create namespace "$NAMESPACE" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

source "$(dirname "$ENV_FILE")/core-secret.sh"
core_secret_create_args=()
ensure_core_secret

echo "==> Creating MCP secret '$NAMESPACE/commoncal-mcp-secrets'..."
# MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER_HOLD is optional: when set, the MCP server holds the new
# issuer (accepts tokens from it) without making it primary (no cutover).
MCP_SECRET_ARGS=(
  --from-literal=mcp-internal-api-key="$MCP_INTERNAL_API_KEY"
  --from-literal=mcp-session-secret="$MCP_SESSION_SECRET"
  --from-literal=mcp-oauth-issuer="$MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER"
)
if [[ -n "${MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER_HOLD:-}" ]]; then
  MCP_SECRET_ARGS+=(--from-literal=mcp-oauth-issuer-hold="$MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER_HOLD")
fi
kubectl create secret generic commoncal-mcp-secrets \
  "${MCP_SECRET_ARGS[@]}" \
  -n "$NAMESPACE" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

echo "==> Creating auth secret '$NAMESPACE/commoncal-auth-secrets'..."
# The authorization server's secrets. The chart never creates this Secret;
# it is created here out-of-band and referenced by the Helm chart.
source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/auth-secret.sh"
apply_auth_secret "$NAMESPACE" apply -f -

echo "==> Bootstrapping Flux (path: deploy/flux/overlays/production)..."
# flux v2.9.4 reads the PAT from the GITHUB_TOKEN env var (loaded above) and
# uses it when --token-auth is set (instead of an SSH deploy key).
flux bootstrap github \
  --owner="$FLUX_OWNER" \
  --repository="$FLUX_REPO" \
  --namespace=flux-system \
  --token-auth \
  --path=deploy/flux/overlays/production \
  --version="$FLUX_VERSION"

echo "==> Waiting for Flux reconciliation..."
sleep 5
flux reconcile kustomization flux-system --namespace=flux-system

echo "==> Verifying resources..."
echo "HelmRelease status:"
flux get helmreleases -A
echo ""
echo "Kustomization status:"
flux get kustomizations -A
echo ""
echo "Workloads:"
kubectl get statefulset,deployment,ingress -n "$NAMESPACE"
echo ""
echo "==> Bootstrap complete."
echo "    Namespace: $NAMESPACE"
echo "    Core domain: $DOMAIN"
echo "    MCP domain: $MCP_DOMAIN"
echo "    TLS secret: $TLS_SECRET_NAME"

<content>
1: # Deployment Guide
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: 
5: Auth, Core, and MCP are deployed to Kubernetes via Flux GitOps. Images are
6: published to GHCR and promoted by an immutable Git commit referencing the
7: exact `sha-<40 hex commit>` that CI built and scanned.
8: 
9: The auth server is a Node.js OIDC provider retained for a future authentication
10: cutover. Its HelmRelease manifest is retained for future use but excluded from
11: the production Kustomization because its PostgreSQL dependency is unavailable.
12: Core therefore deploys without an auth dependency or private bridge
13: configuration, and MCP continues to use its existing issuer.
14: 
15: ## Promotion model
16: 
17: Every push to `main` triggers CI. CI builds and scans all three images
18: (auth, core, MCP). On success, the `promote-main.yml` workflow publishes
19: `main` and `sha-<commit>` tags for all three images, then atomically commits
20: the immutable SHA tag to all three HelmReleases. Flux reconciles that commit.
21: 
22: - Pull-request runs cannot publish or promote images.
23: - Auth, Core, and MCP advance together in one promotion commit.
24: - Workloads use immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tags; `main` is only a
25:   registry convenience tag.
26: - The bot-commit guard prevents promotion loops when the promotion commit
27:   itself triggers a new run.
28: - The latest-main race guard ensures only the current HEAD of main is promoted.
29: 
30: ### Event flow
31: 
32: ```
33: push to main
34:   → CI (checks + deploy-validation) runs
35:   → promote-main.yml triggers (only on push to main, not PR)
36:   → CI builds and scans all three images
37:   → CI publishes main + sha-<commit> for all three images
38:   → CI verifies all registry manifests
39:   → CI commits all three immutable tags to main (bot guard active)
40:   → Flux Kustomization reconciles the commit
41:   → active HelmReleases upgrade (core → mcp; auth remains excluded)
42:   → Kubernetes rolls out new pods
43: ```
44: 
45: ## Architecture
46: 
47: ```
48: Browser ──(Cloudflare)──► Ingress ──► core (StatefulSet)
49:                                            │
50:                                            └──► mcp (Deployment)
51: 
52: auth (HelmRelease excluded; no installed resources or core bridge wiring)
53: ```
54: 
55: - **auth** — Node.js OIDC provider HelmRelease retained in Git, but excluded
56:   from production while managed PostgreSQL is unavailable.
57: - **core** — Rust StatefulSet. The application backend; currently has no auth
58:   HelmRelease dependency or auth bridge configuration. Also serves the
59:   CalDAV account surface (`/dav/`) used by Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS;
60:   see [Connect an Apple Calendar client](#connect-an-apple-calendar-client).
61: - **mcp** — Rust Deployment. The MCP server. Depends on core and continues to
62:   use the existing OAuth issuer (the auth issuer has not been cut over).
63: 
64: ## Namespace
65: 
66: Core and MCP deploy to the `commoncal` namespace. Auth resources are absent
67: while the auth HelmRelease is excluded from production.
68: 
69: Flux is the normal production deployment authority. Active HelmReleases use
70: the explicit release names `commoncal` and `commoncal-mcp`; this avoids Flux's
71: cross-namespace `commoncal-commoncal` default.
72: 
73: Reconcile Flux directly while auth is excluded; `deploy/deploy-prod.sh` still
74: supports the legacy three-release and direct-Helm workflows. Flux deploys the
75: image tags and chart values committed to its Git source, so local `IMAGE_TAG`
76: and direct chart overrides do not affect Flux reconciliation.
77: 
78: ### TLS model (two-hop)
79: 
80: Production TLS uses a two-hop model:
81: 
82: 1. **Browser → Cloudflare edge:** Cloudflare Universal SSL provides a
83:    publicly-trusted certificate for `*.hajnal.space`. Cloudflare must proxy
84:    both DNS records (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`) and use
85:    SSL/TLS mode **Full** (not `Flexible` or `Full (strict)`).
86: 2. **Cloudflare → origin (Traefik):** the origin presents a self-signed
87:    certificate stored in the `commoncal-tls` Kubernetes Secret. Cloudflare in
88:    `Full` mode does not validate the origin certificate — it only requires
89:    that the origin speaks TLS.
90: 
91: The deploy script manages the origin Secret:
92: 
93: - **First run:** if `commoncal-tls` is absent or invalid, the script generates
94:   a self-signed RSA 2048-bit / SHA-256 certificate (365 days) covering both
95:   `DOMAIN` and `MCP_DOMAIN`, and creates the Secret in the `commoncal`
96:   namespace. The private key is never logged.
97: - **Subsequent runs:** if a valid Secret already exists (correct type,
98:   matching key, both SANs present, more than 30 days to expiry), the script
99:   reuses it and does not regenerate.
100: - **30-day expiry guard:** if the existing certificate expires within 30 days,
101:   the script regenerates it.
102: - **Manual rotation:** delete the Secret (`kubectl delete secret commoncal-tls
103:   -n commoncal`) and re-run the deploy script to force regeneration.
104: 
105: No cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, or ACME dependency is required.
106: 
107: The MCP NetworkPolicy allows egress HTTPS to non-private IPv4 addresses only.
108: On a dual-stack cluster, make sure the OAuth issuer and the core domain resolve
109: to IPv4 for MCP egress.
110: 
111: ## Connect an MCP client
112: 
113: After the MCP HelmRelease has reconciled and `/health/ready` succeeds, connect
114: clients to the public streamable-HTTP endpoint:
115: 
116: ```
117: https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp
118: ```
119: 
120: Use a client that supports OAuth-protected MCP servers and streamable HTTP.
121: Give it the endpoint above; it must discover resource metadata at:
122: 
123: ```
124: https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
125: ```
126: 
127: The client should then start its OAuth authorization flow with the issuer
128: advertised by that metadata. Do not copy an access token into a configuration
129: file or share it between users. The client sends its user-specific bearer token
130: with each `POST /mcp` request; the server resolves that user's grant from
131: CommonCal core and only exposes permitted calendars and tools.
132: 
133: For a manual smoke test, use an MCP Inspector or another OAuth-capable MCP
134: client, complete sign-in in its browser window, and run `tools/list`. Then use
135: `calendar_list` to confirm the client sees only calendars covered by its MCP
136: grant. If discovery or login fails, first verify:
137: 
138: ```bash
139: curl -fsS https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
140: curl -fsSI https://mcal.hajnal.space/health/ready
141: ```
142: 
143: `/health/ready` returning `200` confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable; it does
144: not validate a specific user's OAuth grant. Grant failures must be diagnosed in
145: the MCP client or CommonCal core, without logging or pasting bearer tokens.
146: 
147: For an emergency direct deployment, first suspend all three Flux HelmReleases,
148: then run the same script. With all releases suspended (or absent), it deploys
149: all three workloads directly with Helm and requires `IMAGE_TAG` set to an
150: immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tag. It ensures the `commoncal-tls` TLS
151: Secret exists and is valid (generating a self-signed certificate on first run
152: if needed), then deploys all Ingresses referencing that Secret. Resume Flux
153: only after reconciling the direct deployment back into Git. A mixed state with
154: any active HelmRelease is rejected to prevent split ownership.
155: 
156: ## Connect an Apple Calendar client
157: 
158: Core exposes a real two-way CalDAV account surface on the same origin as the
159: web app. Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS connects to it as a standard CalDAV
160: account; Happening is the source of truth and never receives Apple
161: Account/iCloud credentials.
162: 
163: The DAV root is:
164: 
165: ```
166: https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
167: ```
168: 
169: Discovery accepts GET, HEAD and PROPFIND at `/.well-known/caldav` and returns
170: 307 with `Cache-Control: no-cache` to the canonical `/dav/` root.
171: [RFC 6764 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6764#section-5) permits 307;
172: [RFC 9110 §15.4.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-15.4.8)
173: preserves the method and body when following it. Native Apple behavior still
174: requires a client check. No fallback aliases are added for `/` or `/principals/`.
175: At the DAV root, `OPTIONS` advertises the `1, 2, access-control, calendar-access`
176: capabilities, and the principal/calendar-home `PROPFIND` responses expose the
177: user's active calendars with their names, colors, and role privileges.
178: 
179: ### Issue a connection password
180: 
181: Connection passwords are revocable, per-device secrets. They are shown once
182: at creation and stored only as a domain-separated keyed HMAC; the plaintext is never persisted
183: or logged.
184: 
185: From the web app, open **Settings → Calendar connections** and create a
186: password for the device. The API equivalent is:
187: 
188: ```bash
189: # Issue a new connection password (returns the plaintext once).
190: curl -fsS -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords \
191:   -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
192:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>' \
193:   -d '{"label":"My iPhone"}'
194: ```
195: 
196: The response carries the `username` (the account email), the one-time
197: `password`, and the `server_url` to enter in the device.
198: 
199: ### Add the account on the device
200: 
201: - **macOS:** System Settings → Internet Accounts → Add Account → Other CalDAV
202:   Account. Server `cal.hajnal.space`, username the account email, password the
203:   one-time secret.
204: - **iOS:** Settings → Mail → Accounts → Add Account → Other → Other CalDAV
205:   Account. Same server, username, and password.
206: 
207: The device then performs discovery, lists the calendars, and syncs events.
208: Initial sync is a full `sync-collection` snapshot; subsequent syncs are
209: incremental and carry an opaque sync token. Supported CRUD (create, update,
210: delete) and all-day and recurring events round-trip through the domain
211: services, so changes made in Apple Calendar appear in Happening and vice
212: versa.
213: 
214: ### Revoke a connection
215: 
216: Revoking a password immediately invalidates it; the next DAV request from that
217: device fails with `401`. Revoking one device's password does not affect the
218: others.
219: 
220: ```bash
221: # Revoke a single connection password.
222: curl -fsS -X DELETE \
223:   https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords/<id> \
224:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
225: 
226: # Disconnect all devices (revokes every active password).
227: curl -fsS -X DELETE https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple \
228:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
229: ```
230: 
231: To verify a revocation took effect, a DAV request with the old credentials
232: must return `401`:
233: 
234: ```bash
235: curl -fsSI -u '<email>:<old-password>' https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
236: # expect: HTTP/2 401
237: ```
238: 
239: ### Deployment notes
240: 
241: - The CalDAV surface shares the core origin and the two-hop TLS model
242:   described above; no separate certificate or ingress is required.
243: - DAV authentication is rate-limited independently of the browser/API routes,
244:   and request bodies and REPORT payloads are bounded. Logs are redacted and
245:   never contain credentials or event bodies.
246: - Public ICS/WebCal export is a one-off convenience and is **not** the
247:   account-level CalDAV synchronization described here.
248: 
249: ## Images
250: 
251: - Auth: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth`
252: - Core: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core`
253: - MCP: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp`
254: 
255: Tags are `main` (convenience) and `sha-<40 hex commit>` (immutable, production).
256: Version-based tags (`vX.Y.Z`) are retired; they no longer build images or
257: promote production.
258: 
259: ## Pin to a Known-Good SHA
260: 
261: To pin to a known-good version:
262: 
263: 1. Find the promotion commit for the desired SHA:
264:    ```bash
265:    git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
266:    ```
267: 
268: 2. Edit all three HelmRelease tags to the known-good immutable SHA:
269:    ```yaml
270:    # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml
271:    image:
272:      tag: "sha-abc123def456..."
273: 
274:    # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/core-helmrelease.yaml
275:    image:
276:      tag: "sha-abc123def456..."
277: 
278:    # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/mcp-helmrelease.yaml
279:    image:
280:      tag: "sha-abc123def456..."
281:    ```
282: 
283: 3. Commit and push to `main`.
284: 
285: 4. Flux will reconcile within 10 minutes.
286: 
287: ## Reconcile Resources
288: 
289: ```bash
290: # Reconcile all Flux resources
291: flux reconcile kustomization flux-system --namespace=flux-system
292: 
293: # Reconcile specific HelmRelease
294: flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal --namespace=flux-system
295: flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal-mcp --namespace=flux-system
296: ```
297: 
298: ## Revert Promotion Commit
299: 
300: To revert an image promotion:
301: 
302: 1. Find the promotion commit:
303:    ```bash
304:    git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
305:    ```
306: 
307: 2. Revert the commit:
308:    ```bash
309:    git revert <commit-hash>
310:    git push
311:    ```
312: 
313: 3. Flux will reconcile and roll back to the previous version.
314: 
315: ## GHCR Credentials
316: 
317: Images are published to `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/`. `GHCR_TOKEN` in `deploy/.env`
318: only applies to direct Helm deployments; under Flux ownership the script rejects
319: it. If the packages are private, create a Kubernetes pull Secret:
320: 
321: ```bash
322: kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-credentials \
323:   --namespace=commoncal \
324:   --docker-server=ghcr.io \
325:   --docker-username=<username> \
326:   --docker-password=<token> \
327:   --docker-email=<email>
328: ```
329: 
330: Then add to each HelmRelease's `imagePullSecrets`.
331: 
332: ## Production Secrets
333: 
334: - `commoncal-auth-secrets` — auth server secrets:
335:   - `DATABASE_URL` — PostgreSQL connection string for the auth database
336:   - `LAB_BRIDGE_KEY` — shared secret for the private bridge endpoint
337:   - `AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS` — JSON array of cookie signing keys (for rotation)
338:   - `AUTH_SIGNING_KID` — current signing key ID
339: - `commoncal-session` — session encryption (key: `SESSION_SECRET`) and backup encryption (key: `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`)
340: - `commoncal-mcp-secrets` — the shared internal API key, MCP session secret, and HTTPS OAuth issuer (`mcp-oauth-issuer`)
341: - `commoncal-tls` — self-signed TLS certificate for the origin hop (covers both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`)
342: 
343: The shared certificate covers both the core and MCP domains. Both Ingresses
344: reference the same Secret. Browsers receive Cloudflare Universal SSL; the
345: self-signed certificate is only presented on the Cloudflare-to-origin hop.
346: 
347: `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX` must be an even number of hexadecimal characters (at least 32); 64-hex (32-byte) keys remain backward-compatible.
348: 
349: ## Auth Migration
350: 
351: The auth server uses a managed PostgreSQL database. Schema migrations run
352: automatically via a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade Job in the `commoncal-auth`
353: chart. The migration Job:
354: 
355: 1. Runs before the auth Deployment starts
356: 2. Applies all pending migrations in order
357: 3. Exits 0 on success, non-zero on failure
358: 4. Blocks the auth Deployment rollout on failure
359: 
360: To run migrations manually (e.g., after a failed rollout):
361: 
362: ```bash
363: kubectl create job --namespace=commoncal \
364:   --from=cronjob/commoncal-auth-migrate \
365:   commoncal-auth-migrate-manual
366: kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate-manual --follow
367: ```
368: 
369: To inspect migration status:
370: 
371: ```bash
372: kubectl get jobs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-auth
373: kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate --tail=50
374: ```
375: 
376: ## Issuer Cutover
377: 
378: The MCP OAuth issuer is held at `mcp-oauth-issuer` (the MCP server's own
379: issuer) until the auth server is fully operational. The cutover to the auth
380: server's issuer is an explicit, manual step:
381: 
382: 1. **Verify the auth server is healthy:**
383:    ```bash
384:    curl -s https://auth.hajnal.space/.well-known/openid-configuration
385:    ```
386: 
387: 2. **Update the MCP issuer:**

425: ## TLS Cutover Checklist
426: 
427: Execute in this exact order. Each step must succeed before proceeding to the
428: next.
429: 
430: ### Pre-cutover
431: 
432: 1. **Confirm proxied DNS.** Both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`
433:    must be proxied (orange cloud) in Cloudflare:
434:    ```bash
435:    dig +short A cal.hajnal.space    # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
436:    dig +short A mcal.hajnal.space   # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
437:    ```
438: 2. **Set Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode to `Full`.** In the Cloudflare dashboard
439:    (SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin), select **Full**.
440:    - Do **not** use `Full (strict)` — it validates the origin certificate and
441:      will reject the self-signed cert with error **526**.
442:    - Do **not** use `Flexible` — it allows plain-HTTP origin traffic, which
443:      breaks HSTS and the HTTPS-only OAuth flow required by both applications.
444: 3. **Back up the existing TLS Secret** (if one exists):
445:    ```bash
446:    kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal -o yaml \
447:      > commoncal-tls-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml
448:    ```
449: 
450: ### Cutover
451: 
452: 4. **Deploy.** Run the deploy script (Flux or direct mode):
453:    ```bash
454:    bash deploy/deploy-prod.sh
455:    ```
456:    On first run this generates the self-signed certificate and creates the
457:    `commoncal-tls` Secret. On subsequent runs it reuses the existing Secret.
458: 
459: 5. **Verify both edge endpoints** (browser-facing, Cloudflare Universal SSL):
460:    ```bash
461:    curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space | head -5
462:    curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
463:    ```
464:    Both must return `200` or `301`/`302` with a valid TLS handshake.
465: 
466: 6. **Verify direct-origin SNI** (Cloudflare-to-origin hop, self-signed):
467:    ```bash
468:    ORIGIN_IP=<k3s-node-public-ip>
469:    openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
470:      | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
471:    openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
472:      | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
473:    ```
474:    Both must present a self-signed certificate containing both SANs
475:    (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`).
476: 
477: 7. **Inspect logs.** Check for TLS errors in the ingress controller and
478:    application logs:
479:    ```bash
480:    kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik --tail=50
481:    kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal --tail=50
482:    kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp --tail=50
483:    ```
484:    No TLS handshake errors, no 526/521/525 Cloudflare error codes.
485: 
486: ### Post-cutover (optional)
487: 
488: 8. **Delete cluster cert-manager resources (optional).** Only if cert-manager
489:    is no longer needed by any other workload:
490:    ```bash
491:    # First: inventory all Certificate and ClusterIssuer resources
492:    kubectl get certificates -A
493:    kubectl get clusterissuers
494:    ```
495:    If no other Certificate resources exist, you may uninstall cert-manager:
496:    ```bash
497:    helm uninstall cert-manager -n cert-manager
498:    kubectl delete namespace cert-manager
499:    kubectl delete crd certificates.cert-manager.io
500:    kubectl delete crd challengers.cert-manager.io
501:    kubectl delete crd orders.cert-manager.io
502:    kubectl delete crd issuers.cert-manager.io
503:    kubectl delete crd clusterissuers.cert-manager.io
504:    ```
505:    **Do not delete cert-manager if any other Certificate resource depends on
506:    it.**

509: 
510: If the cutover must be reverted:
511: 
512: 1. Restore the previous trusted TLS Secret:
513:    ```bash
514:    kubectl apply -f commoncal-tls-backup-<date>.yaml
515:    ```
516: 2. Switch Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode back to the previous mode (typically
517:    **Full (strict)** if a trusted cert was in place before):

519: 3. Verify both domains:

624: ## Ad-hoc SQLite Console
625: 
626: Open a read-only SQLite console on the production database:
627: 
628: ```bash
629: sudo ./deploy/sqlite-prod.sh
630: ```
631: 
632: Open a writable console (requires typed confirmation):
633: 
634: ```bash
635: sudo ./deploy/sqlite-prod.sh --write
636: ```
637: 
638: ### Requirements
639: 
640: - Run from an SSH session on the production server
641: - `kubectl` installed and configured with local k3s kubeconfig (`/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml`)
642: - Root access (`sudo`)
643: - Interactive terminal (tty)
644: 
645: ### Safety
646: 
647: - Read-only is the default
648: - Write mode requires typing the pod name exactly to confirm
649: - The console pod is automatically cleaned up on exit, Ctrl-C, or after 1 hour
650: - Only one console session is allowed at a time
651: - The pod has no network connectivity (deny-all NetworkPolicy)
652: - The pod runs as non-root UID 1000 with a read-only root filesystem
653: - The live database PVC is mounted directly; no database files are copied
654: 
655: ### Troubleshooting
656: 
657: - **Pod fails to start**: Check PVC attachment — `kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n commoncal`
658: - **Another session active**: `kubectl delete pod commoncal-sqlite-console -n commoncal`
659: - **NetworkPolicy missing**: Deploy the Helm chart or create the policy manually
660: - **Database not found**: The database file must exist on the core pod before opening a console
661: - **`attempt to write a readonly database (8)`**: The console pod is a *separate* pod
662:   mounting the same PVC. SQLite in WAL mode needs to write the `-wal`/`-shm`
663:   files, whose ownership (UID 1000, held by the live core pod) the console pod
664:   cannot match — so writes fail even in `--write` mode. For one-off writes,
665:   exec directly into the core pod instead (see below).
666: 
667: ## MCP Database Backup and Restore
668: 
669: The MCP server keeps its local state in one SQLite file:
670: 
671: - **Path in the pod**: `/app/data/mcp-server.db` (WAL mode, so `-wal`/`-shm`
672:   sidecar files may exist alongside it)
673: - **PVC**: `commoncal-mcp-data` in the `commoncal` namespace
674:   (`ReadWriteOnce`, retained on Helm uninstall)
675: - **Deployment**: `commoncal-mcp`, **exactly one replica** — SQLite allows a
676:   single writer, and the Helm chart schema rejects any other replica count.
677:   Never run two MCP pods against the same PVC.
678: 
679: The production image ships the `sqlite3` CLI for the procedures below.
680: 
681: ### Backup (online, service stays up)
682: 
683: `VACUUM INTO` produces a consistent snapshot of a live WAL database:
684: 
685: ```bash
686: POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
687:   -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
688: 
689: # Consistent snapshot while the service keeps serving
690: kubectl exec -n commoncal "$POD" -- \
691:   sqlite3 /app/data/mcp-server.db "VACUUM INTO '/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db';"
692: 
693: # Pull the snapshot out of the pod
694: kubectl cp "commoncal/$POD:/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db" ./mcp-server-backup.db
695: 
696: # Verify the snapshot before trusting it
697: sqlite3 ./mcp-server-backup.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"   # must print ok
698: ```
699: 
700: ### Restore (service must be stopped)
701: 
702: The single writer must be down while the database file is replaced:
703: 
704: ```bash
705: # 1. Stop the single writer (the PVC is retained)
706: kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=0
707: 
708: # 2. Start a temporary pod on the retained PVC
709: kubectl run mcp-restore -n commoncal --rm -it --restart=Never \
710:   --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep infinity \
711:   --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"mcp-restore","volumeMounts":[{"name":"data","mountPath":"/app/data"}]}],"volumes":[{"name":"data","persistentVolumeClaim":{"claimName":"commoncal-mcp-data"}}]}}'
712: 
713: # 3. Replace the database file, clear WAL sidecars, and fix ownership
714: #    (the MCP pod runs as UID 1000)
715: kubectl cp ./mcp-server-backup.db commoncal/mcp-restore:/app/data/mcp-server.db
716: kubectl exec -n commoncal mcp-restore -- sh -c \
717:   'chown 1000:1000 /app/data/mcp-server.db && rm -f /app/data/mcp-server.db-wal /app/data/mcp-server.db-shm'
718: 
719: # 4. Remove the temporary pod and start the service
720: kubectl delete pod mcp-restore -n commoncal
721: kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=1
722: ```
723: 
724: ### Verify after restore
725: 
726: ```bash
727: POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
728:   -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
729: 
730: # Database integrity — must print ok
731: kubectl exec -n commoncal "$POD" -- \
732:   sqlite3 /app/data/mcp-server.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
733: 
734: # Service readiness — /health/ready confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable
735: kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp
736: curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
737: ```

739: ## Change the admin password
740: 
741: There is no `set-password` CLI command or HTTP endpoint. The password is a
742: bcrypt hash (cost 12) stored in `users.password_hash`, matched by
743: `normalized_email`. The default admin row is `admin@localhost`.
744: 
745: > **Do not use `deploy/sqlite-prod.sh --write` for this.** The console pod
746: > hits `attempt to write a readonly database (8)` (WAL/SHM ownership, see
747: > Troubleshooting above). Run the write inside the **core pod**, which already
748: > holds the database open and has write access.
749: 
750: ### 1. Generate a bcrypt hash (cost 12)
751: 
752: ```bash
753: # Option A: python3 + bcrypt
754: HASH=$(python3 -c 'import bcrypt; print(bcrypt.hashpw(b"NEW_PASSWORD", bcrypt.gensalt(12)).decode())')
755: 
756: # Option B: htpasswd (strip the "user:" prefix)
757: # HASH=$(htpasswd -BbnC 12 admin NEW_PASSWORD | cut -d: -f2)
758: 
759: echo "$HASH"   # sanity check: 60 chars, starts with $2b$12$ / $2y$12$
760: ```
761: 
762: ### 2. Write it into the core pod's database
763: 
764: ```bash
765: kubectl exec -n commoncal commoncal-0 -- \
766:   sqlite3 /app/data/commoncal.sqlite \
767:   "PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000; UPDATE users SET password_hash='$HASH' WHERE normalized_email='admin@localhost'; SELECT changes();"
768: ```
769: 
770: `SELECT changes();` must print `1`. If it prints `0`, the email did not match —
771: check the row with `SELECT normalized_email FROM users;`.
772: 
773: > **Quoting:** the hash is passed as the value of the shell variable `$HASH`,
774: > so its `$` characters are **not** re-expanded by the shell (variable
775: > expansion is not recursive). If you inline a literal hash inside the
776: > double-quoted SQL string instead, you must escape every `$` as `\$` or the
777: > shell will mangle it.
778: 
779: ### 3. Enable password login and restart the pod
780: 
781: Password login is **off by default in production** (`password_login_enabled`
782: defaults to `false`); the `POST /api/v1/auth/password-login` route is only
783: registered when it is `true`. Set the env var and restart so the pod picks it
784: up:
785: 
786: ```bash
787: # Quick one-liner (Flux will revert unless you also update Helm values):
788: k -n commoncal set env statefulset/commoncal PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED=true
789: k -n commoncal rollout restart statefulset commoncal
790: 
791: # Or via ConfigMap:
792: kubectl -n commoncal patch configmap commoncal \
793:   --type merge -p '{"data":{"PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED":"1"}}'}
794: kubectl -n commoncal rollout restart statefulset commoncal
795: ```
796: 
797: > **Flux reverts bare `kubectl` edits.** The durable fix is to add
798: > `PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED: "1"` to the Helm values source
799: > (`deploy/helm/commoncal/templates/configmap.yaml` /
800: > `deploy/values-production.yaml`) and let Flux reconcile it, or the patch
801: > above will be rolled back on the next reconciliation.
802: 
803: ### 4. Verify
804: 
805: ```bash
806: curl -s -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/auth/password-login \
807:   -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
808:   -d '{"email":"admin@localhost","password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}'
809: ```
810: 
811: A `405 Method Not Allowed` means the route is not registered — the env var did
812: not reach the running pod (Flux reverted the ConfigMap, or the pod has not
813: restarted). Confirm with
814: `kubectl -n commoncal get configmap commoncal -o yaml | grep PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED`
815: and `kubectl -n commoncal get pods`.

818: ## CalDAV compatibility repair handoff
819: 
820: Code-level verification is separate from native Apple account setup. No
821: successful macOS setup or production rollout is established by the local tests.
822: 
823: The repair covers these defects:
824: 
825: - Missing/unsupported properties and propname now use namespace-preserving XML
826:   elements; empty status groups are omitted and explicit selections are honored.
827: - XML parsing restores namespace scope and validates document/report grammar;
828:   object PROPFIND, authenticated principal metadata, Depth rules and report
829:   property selection share the corrected property handling.
830: - Calendar-query applies component/range/recurrence semantics and reports result
831:   overflow. Unsupported filters or calendar-data projections fail explicitly.
832: - Sync tokens are direct multistatus children, collection/user/visibility-bound
833:   opaque URIs. Snapshots retain their high-water mark, pages continue explicitly,
834:   changes coalesce by resource, and durable tombstones survive event deletion.
835:   Concurrent writes can require retry (503); old tokens require full resync
836:   (403 `DAV:valid-sync-token`). Migration `0028_caldav_visibility_epochs.sql`
837:   persists ACL epochs so revoke/regrant cannot revive a previous token.
838: - HTTP status/capability/privilege claims, write preconditions and validators,
839:   and iCalendar escaping, folding and timezone representation are corrected.
840:   Parsing respects quoted parameter delimiters and escaped commas in categories;
841:   URL properties retain URI values. Imported metadata is persisted and existing
842:   imports are backfilled on a successful HTTP 200 feed refresh.
843: 
844: ### Post-deployment checks
845: 
846: After the normal release applies migration 0028, run the read-only semantic
847: smoke from the repository root. Enter a newly generated device password at the
848: hidden prompt; do not paste credentials into command arguments or enable shell
849: tracing. The script follows advertised same-origin principal/home/collection
850: URLs, validates XML property statuses and checks initial-sync continuations.
851: 
852: ```sh
853: export CALDAV_ORIGIN=https://cal.hajnal.space
854: read -r -p 'Happening email: ' CALDAV_USERNAME
855: export CALDAV_USERNAME
856: read -r -s -p 'Connection password: ' CALDAV_PASSWORD
857: printf '\n'
858: export CALDAV_PASSWORD
859: python3 scripts/caldav-smoke.py
860: unset CALDAV_USERNAME CALDAV_PASSWORD
861: ```
862: 
863: The prompts above use bash (`bash` first if your interactive shell is zsh).
864: Success prints a calendar count, never credentials. A nonzero exit means the
865: smoke failed; inspect server-side status logs without printing request headers.
866: This smoke does not test write operations or prove native Apple compatibility.
867: 
868: Then add a new Other CalDAV Account on macOS using the server, Happening email
869: and a fresh connection password. Confirm account acceptance, expected writable,
870: read-only and free/busy calendars, first sync and subsequent refresh. On a test
871: calendar, create/read/update/delete an event in each app and verify the other
872: app receives every change; include an all-day event and recurrence exception.
873: Check imported-event restrictions and revoke a test connection to confirm 401.
874: Record macOS version, setup time and result; do not record the password.
875: 
876: If account setup still fails, capture the corresponding reverse-proxy access
877: records with only timestamp, request **method**, URL **path** (without query),
878: response **status**, and **User-Agent**. Keep Authorization, Cookie, passwords,
879: request/response bodies and token-bearing query strings out of logs and shared
880: traces. Correlate the setup time and User-Agent with discovery, PROPFIND and
881: REPORT requests; inspect individual propstat statuses for 207 responses. This
882: is a capture procedure, not a claim that safe logging is already configured.
883: 
884: Residual checks: native Apple request sequences, TLS/public-host redirects and
885: production middleware remain deployment checks; concurrent workloads may need
886: 503 retries and token-format changes cause a one-time full resync. The bundled
887: chrono-tz transition data ends in 2099; recurring schedules beyond that horizon
888: need refreshed timezone data before relying on future DST behavior. Local test
889: results belong in the accompanying change report, including unavailable checks.

892: [RFC 3744 (privileges/principals)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3744),
893: [RFC 4791 (CalDAV)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4791),

895: [RFC 6764 (discovery)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6764),
896: [RFC 6578 (sync)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6578),

# Deployment Guide

## Overview

Auth, Core, and MCP are deployed to Kubernetes via Flux GitOps. Images are
published to GHCR and promoted by an immutable Git commit referencing the
exact `sha-<40 hex commit>` that CI built and scanned.

The auth server is a Node.js OIDC provider retained for a future authentication
cutover. Its HelmRelease manifest is retained for future use but excluded from
the production Kustomization because its PostgreSQL dependency is unavailable.
Core therefore deploys without an auth dependency or private bridge
configuration, and MCP continues to use its existing issuer.

## Promotion model

Every push to `main` triggers CI. CI builds and scans all three images
(auth, core, MCP). On success, the `promote-main.yml` workflow publishes
`main` and `sha-<commit>` tags for all three images, then atomically commits
the immutable SHA tag to all three HelmReleases. Flux reconciles that commit.

- Pull-request runs cannot publish or promote images.
- Auth, Core, and MCP advance together in one promotion commit.
- Workloads use immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tags; `main` is only a
  registry convenience tag.
- The bot-commit guard prevents promotion loops when the promotion commit
  itself triggers a new run.
- The latest-main race guard ensures only the current HEAD of main is promoted.

### Event flow

```
push to main
  → CI (checks + deploy-validation) runs
  → promote-main.yml triggers (only on push to main, not PR)
  → CI builds and scans all three images
  → CI publishes main + sha-<commit> for all three images
  → CI verifies all registry manifests
  → CI commits all three immutable tags to main (bot guard active)
  → Flux Kustomization reconciles the commit
  → active HelmReleases upgrade (core → mcp; auth remains excluded)
  → Kubernetes rolls out new pods
```

## Architecture

```
Browser ──(Cloudflare)──► Ingress ──► core (StatefulSet)
                                           │
                                           └──► mcp (Deployment)

auth (HelmRelease excluded; no installed resources or core bridge wiring)
```

- **auth** — Node.js OIDC provider HelmRelease retained in Git, but excluded
  from production while managed PostgreSQL is unavailable.
- **core** — Rust StatefulSet. The application backend; currently has no auth
  HelmRelease dependency or auth bridge configuration. Also serves the
  CalDAV account surface (`/dav/`) used by Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS;
  see [Connect an Apple Calendar client](#connect-an-apple-calendar-client).
- **mcp** — Rust Deployment. The MCP server. Depends on core and continues to
  use the existing OAuth issuer (the auth issuer has not been cut over).

## Namespace

Core and MCP deploy to the `commoncal` namespace. Auth resources are absent
while the auth HelmRelease is excluded from production.

Flux is the normal production deployment authority. Active HelmReleases use
the explicit release names `commoncal` and `commoncal-mcp`; this avoids Flux's
cross-namespace `commoncal-commoncal` default.

Reconcile Flux directly while auth is excluded; `deploy/deploy-prod.sh` still
supports the legacy three-release and direct-Helm workflows. Flux deploys the
image tags and chart values committed to its Git source, so local `IMAGE_TAG`
and direct chart overrides do not affect Flux reconciliation.

### TLS model (two-hop)

Production TLS uses a two-hop model:

1. **Browser → Cloudflare edge:** Cloudflare Universal SSL provides a
   publicly-trusted certificate for `*.hajnal.space`. Cloudflare must proxy
   both DNS records (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`) and use
   SSL/TLS mode **Full** (not `Flexible` or `Full (strict)`).
2. **Cloudflare → origin (Traefik):** the origin presents a self-signed
   certificate stored in the `commoncal-tls` Kubernetes Secret. Cloudflare in
   `Full` mode does not validate the origin certificate — it only requires
   that the origin speaks TLS.

The deploy script manages the origin Secret:

- **First run:** if `commoncal-tls` is absent or invalid, the script generates
  a self-signed RSA 2048-bit / SHA-256 certificate (365 days) covering both
  `DOMAIN` and `MCP_DOMAIN`, and creates the Secret in the `commoncal`
  namespace. The private key is never logged.
- **Subsequent runs:** if a valid Secret already exists (correct type,
  matching key, both SANs present, more than 30 days to expiry), the script
  reuses it and does not regenerate.
- **30-day expiry guard:** if the existing certificate expires within 30 days,
  the script regenerates it.
- **Manual rotation:** delete the Secret (`kubectl delete secret commoncal-tls
  -n commoncal`) and re-run the deploy script to force regeneration.

No cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, or ACME dependency is required.

The MCP NetworkPolicy allows egress HTTPS to non-private IPv4 addresses only.
On a dual-stack cluster, make sure the OAuth issuer and the core domain resolve
to IPv4 for MCP egress.

## Connect an MCP client

After the MCP HelmRelease has reconciled and `/health/ready` succeeds, connect
clients to the public streamable-HTTP endpoint:

```
https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp
```

Use a client that supports OAuth-protected MCP servers and streamable HTTP.
Give it the endpoint above; it must discover resource metadata at:

```
https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
```

The client should then start its OAuth authorization flow with the issuer
advertised by that metadata. Do not copy an access token into a configuration
file or share it between users. The client sends its user-specific bearer token
with each `POST /mcp` request; the server resolves that user's grant from
CommonCal core and only exposes permitted calendars and tools.

For a manual smoke test, use an MCP Inspector or another OAuth-capable MCP
client, complete sign-in in its browser window, and run `tools/list`. Then use
`calendar_list` to confirm the client sees only calendars covered by its MCP
grant. If discovery or login fails, first verify:

```bash
curl -fsS https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
curl -fsSI https://mcal.hajnal.space/health/ready
```

`/health/ready` returning `200` confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable; it does
not validate a specific user's OAuth grant. Grant failures must be diagnosed in
the MCP client or CommonCal core, without logging or pasting bearer tokens.

For an emergency direct deployment, first suspend all three Flux HelmReleases,
then run the same script. With all releases suspended (or absent), it deploys
all three workloads directly with Helm and requires `IMAGE_TAG` set to an
immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tag. It ensures the `commoncal-tls` TLS
Secret exists and is valid (generating a self-signed certificate on first run
if needed), then deploys all Ingresses referencing that Secret. Resume Flux
only after reconciling the direct deployment back into Git. A mixed state with
any active HelmRelease is rejected to prevent split ownership.

## Connect an Apple Calendar client

Core exposes a real two-way CalDAV account surface on the same origin as the
web app. Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS connects to it as a standard CalDAV
account; Happening is the source of truth and never receives Apple
Account/iCloud credentials.

The DAV root is:

```
https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
```

Discovery accepts GET, HEAD and PROPFIND at `/.well-known/caldav` and returns
307 with `Cache-Control: no-cache` to the canonical `/dav/` root.
[RFC 6764 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6764#section-5) permits 307;
[RFC 9110 §15.4.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-15.4.8)
preserves the method and body when following it. Native Apple behavior still
requires a client check. No fallback aliases are added for `/` or `/principals/`.
At the DAV root, `OPTIONS` advertises the `1, 2, access-control, calendar-access`
capabilities, and the principal/calendar-home `PROPFIND` responses expose the
user's active calendars with their names, colors, and role privileges.

### Issue a connection password

Connection passwords are revocable, per-device secrets. They are shown once
at creation and stored only as a domain-separated keyed HMAC; the plaintext is never persisted
or logged.

From the web app, open **Settings → Calendar connections** and create a
password for the device. The API equivalent is:

```bash
# Issue a new connection password (returns the plaintext once).
curl -fsS -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>' \
  -d '{"label":"My iPhone"}'
```

The response carries the `username` (the account email), the one-time
`password`, and the `server_url` to enter in the device.

### Add the account on the device

- **macOS:** System Settings → Internet Accounts → Add Account → Other CalDAV
  Account. Server `cal.hajnal.space`, username the account email, password the
  one-time secret.
- **iOS:** Settings → Mail → Accounts → Add Account → Other → Other CalDAV
  Account. Same server, username, and password.

The device then performs discovery, lists the calendars, and syncs events.
Initial sync is a full `sync-collection` snapshot; subsequent syncs are
incremental and carry an opaque sync token. Supported CRUD (create, update,
delete) and all-day and recurring events round-trip through the domain
services, so changes made in Apple Calendar appear in Happening and vice
versa.

### Revoke a connection

Revoking a password immediately invalidates it; the next DAV request from that
device fails with `401`. Revoking one device's password does not affect the
others.

```bash
# Revoke a single connection password.
curl -fsS -X DELETE \
  https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords/<id> \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'

# Disconnect all devices (revokes every active password).
curl -fsS -X DELETE https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
```

To verify a revocation took effect, a DAV request with the old credentials
must return `401`:

```bash
curl -fsSI -u '<email>:<old-password>' https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
# expect: HTTP/2 401
```

### Deployment notes

- The CalDAV surface shares the core origin and the two-hop TLS model
  described above; no separate certificate or ingress is required.
- DAV authentication is rate-limited independently of the browser/API routes,
  and request bodies and REPORT payloads are bounded. Logs are redacted and
  never contain credentials or event bodies.
- Public ICS/WebCal export is a one-off convenience and is **not** the
  account-level CalDAV synchronization described here.

## Images

- Auth: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth`
- Core: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core`
- MCP: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp`

Tags are `main` (convenience) and `sha-<40 hex commit>` (immutable, production).
Version-based tags (`vX.Y.Z`) are retired; they no longer build images or
promote production.

## Pin to a Known-Good SHA

To pin to a known-good version:

1. Find the promotion commit for the desired SHA:
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   ```

2. Edit all three HelmRelease tags to the known-good immutable SHA:
   ```yaml
   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."

   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/core-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."

   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/mcp-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."
   ```

3. Commit and push to `main`.

4. Flux will reconcile within 10 minutes.

## Reconcile Resources

```bash
# Reconcile all Flux resources
flux reconcile kustomization flux-system --namespace=flux-system

# Reconcile specific HelmRelease
flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal --namespace=flux-system
flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal-mcp --namespace=flux-system
```

## Revert Promotion Commit

To revert an image promotion:

1. Find the promotion commit:
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   ```

2. Revert the commit:
   ```bash
   git revert <commit-hash>
   git push
   ```

3. Flux will reconcile and roll back to the previous version.

## GHCR Credentials

Images are published to `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/`. `GHCR_TOKEN` in `deploy/.env`
only applies to direct Helm deployments; under Flux ownership the script rejects
it. If the packages are private, create a Kubernetes pull Secret:

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-credentials \
  --namespace=commoncal \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=<username> \
  --docker-password=<token> \
  --docker-email=<email>
```

Then add to each HelmRelease's `imagePullSecrets`.

## Production Secrets

- `commoncal-auth-secrets` — auth server secrets:
  - `DATABASE_URL` — PostgreSQL connection string for the auth database
  - `LAB_BRIDGE_KEY` — shared secret for the private bridge endpoint
  - `AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS` — JSON array of cookie signing keys (for rotation)
  - `AUTH_SIGNING_KID` — current signing key ID
- `commoncal-session` — session encryption (key: `SESSION_SECRET`) and backup encryption (key: `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`)
- `commoncal-mcp-secrets` — the shared internal API key, MCP session secret, and HTTPS OAuth issuer (`mcp-oauth-issuer`)
- `commoncal-tls` — self-signed TLS certificate for the origin hop (covers both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`)

The shared certificate covers both the core and MCP domains. Both Ingresses
reference the same Secret. Browsers receive Cloudflare Universal SSL; the
self-signed certificate is only presented on the Cloudflare-to-origin hop.

`BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX` must be an even number of hexadecimal characters (at least 32); 64-hex (32-byte) keys remain backward-compatible.

## Auth Migration

The auth server uses a managed PostgreSQL database. Schema migrations run
automatically via a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade Job in the `commoncal-auth`
chart. The migration Job:

1. Runs before the auth Deployment starts
2. Applies all pending migrations in order
3. Exits 0 on success, non-zero on failure
4. Blocks the auth Deployment rollout on failure

To run migrations manually (e.g., after a failed rollout):

```bash
kubectl create job --namespace=commoncal \
  --from=cronjob/commoncal-auth-migrate \
  commoncal-auth-migrate-manual
kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate-manual --follow
```

To inspect migration status:

```bash
kubectl get jobs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-auth
kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate --tail=50
```

## Issuer Cutover

The MCP OAuth issuer is held at `mcp-oauth-issuer` (the MCP server's own
issuer) until the auth server is fully operational. The cutover to the auth
server's issuer is an explicit, manual step:

1. **Verify the auth server is healthy:**
   ```bash
   curl -s https://auth.hajnal.space/.well-known/openid-configuration
   ```

2. **Update the MCP issuer:**
   ```bash
   kubectl -n commoncal patch secret commoncal-mcp-secrets \
     --type merge -p '{"data":{"OAUTH_ISSUER":"https://auth.hajnal.space"}}'
   kubectl -n commoncal rollout restart deployment commoncal-mcp
   ```

3. **Verify MCP OAuth flow:**
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
   ```

> **Warning:** The issuer cutover is irreversible without a rollback. If the
> auth server is not healthy, do not cutover. The MCP server will reject
> tokens from the new issuer if the JWKS endpoint is unreachable.

## Rollback

To roll back a release:

1. **Revert the promotion commit:**
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   git revert <commit-hash>
   git push
   ```

To roll back the auth server specifically:

1. Revert the auth HelmRelease tag to the previous version
2. The migration Job is idempotent — it will not re-run if the schema is
   already at the target version
3. If the migration was destructive, restore the database from backup:
   ```bash
   pg_restore --dbname=commoncal_auth --clean --if-exists \
     --username=auth < backup-file.dump
   ```

## TLS Cutover Checklist

Execute in this exact order. Each step must succeed before proceeding to the
next.

### Pre-cutover

1. **Confirm proxied DNS.** Both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`
   must be proxied (orange cloud) in Cloudflare:
   ```bash
   dig +short A cal.hajnal.space    # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
   dig +short A mcal.hajnal.space   # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
   ```
2. **Set Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode to `Full`.** In the Cloudflare dashboard
   (SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin), select **Full**.
   - Do **not** use `Full (strict)` — it validates the origin certificate and
     will reject the self-signed cert with error **526**.
   - Do **not** use `Flexible` — it allows plain-HTTP origin traffic, which
     breaks HSTS and the HTTPS-only OAuth flow required by both applications.
3. **Back up the existing TLS Secret** (if one exists):
   ```bash
   kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal -o yaml \
     > commoncal-tls-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml
   ```

### Cutover

4. **Deploy.** Run the deploy script (Flux or direct mode):
   ```bash
   bash deploy/deploy-prod.sh
   ```
   On first run this generates the self-signed certificate and creates the
   `commoncal-tls` Secret. On subsequent runs it reuses the existing Secret.

5. **Verify both edge endpoints** (browser-facing, Cloudflare Universal SSL):
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space | head -5
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
   ```
   Both must return `200` or `301`/`302` with a valid TLS handshake.

6. **Verify direct-origin SNI** (Cloudflare-to-origin hop, self-signed):
   ```bash
   ORIGIN_IP=<k3s-node-public-ip>
   openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
     | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
   openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
     | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
   ```
